content:
For the past few weeks, I've been playing with gpt-5.6-luna. It is shockingly capable, fast, and smart. I regularly see it do ~100 tps, and rip around my codebase, email, and knowledge base.

Of course, the biggest thing with luna is the cost. I've tried running some fairly complicated research threads, and it's pretty tough to run up a large bill. Even having it search across thousands of emails, I end up with an API cost in the tens of cents.

Courtesy of artificialanalysis.ai

With GLM 5.3, we even have a new option at the Pareto frontier.

When doing coding work, I almost always reach for the most expensive and capable models (Fable 5, 5.6 Sol). So it's been easy to miss the progress the small fast models have made.

One thing a few investors I've talked with have mentioned: "It's weird we're not seeing more consumer AI companies. Why is that?"

There's a straightforward answer: token costs.

In the times before AI, the playbook for big consumer apps looked like this...

  • create some sort of compelling website which is fairly cheap to run
  • attract a bunch of users (typically with some virality)
  • raise money, scale to more users
  • create an ads marketplace

This roughly describes most of the big consumer companies (Google, Facebook, Snapchat, etc.).1

But what if you want to add AI to your product? Well, now you have some real inference costs on every request! Suddenly the amount of capital required increases dramatically.

A pet eval of mine is to build a daily news site, personalized to me:

research @calvinfo on the internet. figure out what news they might like. build a micro-site with today's top stories, personalized for them. search hn, reddit, twitter, etc.

With the previous generation of models (Sonnet class), you'd spend ~$1 to get anywhere. Charging $30/mo is untenable for a consumer app. There's obviously a lot we can optimize here, but if you're charging what the WSJ or The Economist charges, you'd better be delivering similar value.

But looking at luna, the results are pretty decent, and the average cost is ~$0.10. Now we're talking!

Where I think this gets even more interesting is in the world of business.

My Segment co-founder Peter and I were recently comparing notes on a hike. Across his various startups, Peter has seen two kinds of work:

  1. the "IQ 180" work. some mad scientist genius type comes up with some crazy solution you've never thought of.
  2. the "token spewer" work. being ultra responsive, pushing the ball forward across dozens of different fronts.

Peter runs multiple companies. Beyond Segment, he's raised $100m+ for Charm Industrial, and just recently closed a Series A for Revoy. He's incredibly organized and efficient with his time.

And yet, Peter mentioned that ~95% of the work he does falls into bucket 2. It's hopping on calls. Nudging people. Blocking and tackling.

To be clear, Peter says his companies would be dead-in-the-water today without an IQ 180 technical mind solving the deep problems. Just that most of his work falls in bucket 2.2

I think demand for "frontier-level" models is going to keep compounding. Especially for fields that require novel breakthroughs or discovery (engineering, hard science, model training).

But I also think the demand for "fast/cheap/good-enough" models is just about to take off.

Think of the people you interact with on a daily basis: coworkers, vendors, and customers. Nine times out of ten, you want someone who is super responsive, and just handles things for you. Most of the "human tokens" at companies today are spent this way — hiring skews heavily toward the fast/cheap/good-enough archetype.

There's a lot of work that needs to happen to make fast/cheap/good-enough models a reality for business. New harnesses, prompt injection safety, roles, and permissions. But I'm confident we'll figure that out.

If you're also experimenting with making small models useful, please drop me a line.

Footnotes

  1. Amazon and Netflix are the notable exceptions ↩

  2. Peter is also being modest here. He's sharp as a tack. ↩
articles.summary: The fast/cheap/good-enough models have quietly gotten good. That unlocks consumer AI, and most of the "token spewer" work that actually runs a business.
articles.title: Small Models Have Arrived

1 oz Planteray OFTD Rum
1/2 oz Brugal 1888 Rum (Privateer New England Reserve)
1/2 oz Monkey Shoulder Scotch (3/8 oz Cutty Sark Prohibition + 1/8 oz Laphroaig)
1/2 oz Borghetti Coffee Liqueur
1/2 oz Pineapple Juice
1 oz Coco Lopez

Whip shake, pour into a glass (coconut mug), top with crushed ice, and garnish with 2 pineapple fronds, a banana chip, and freshly grated coffee bean.

Two Wednesdays ago, I opened up the Spec recipe app, and in the Bardtenders podcast's collection, I found the Bad Juju as a Piña Colada riff created by one of the podcast's hosts, Jon Mateer. Jon runs the bar program at TPC Sawgrass golf course in Ponte Vedra Beach, Florida, and perhaps the name refers to one of the cursed holes. One article described, "The phrase 'bad juju' at TPC Sawgrass most famously relates to the notorious water-logged history of the iconic par-3 17th island green, where PGA Tour groups have occasionally suffered collective meltdowns by hitting their tee shots straight into the water." I thought that I had tried a coffee-tinged Piña Colada before, but alas, I had not; the closest was Chad Austin's pineapple-less Aztec Warrior, so the Bad Juju was indeed a first.
Once prepared, the Bad Juju offered up coffee and a hint of smoke on the nose. Next, a creamy sip with roast notes slid into burly rum, hint of smoky Scotch, coconut, pineapple, and coffee flavors on the swallow. Jon commented on my Instagram post, "Love the addition of splitting the Scotch here! That 1/8 of Laphroaig is money," to which I explained that the last of "my Cutty Sark bottle ran short, so I figured to fill the gap with flavor instead of a more neutral blended whisky."

The Go Blog

Generic Methods

Mark Freeman
26 August 2026

Generics was a profound change for Go—it fundamentally expanded the kinds of programs that gophers could write by adding type parameters to the language.

One could now express generic types and functions in Go. These constructs decreased the need for specialized data types and functions, reducing program verbosity and improving the ergonomics of the language in those cases.

To illustrate, different kinds of linked lists could now be condensed into a single type definition:

// before Go 1.18
type ListOfInts struct {
    elem int
    next *ListOfInts
}
type ListOfStrings struct {
    elem string
    next *ListOfStrings
}
// ...

// after Go 1.18
type List[E any] struct {
    elem E
    next *List[E]
}

Likewise, sorting different kinds of ordered data could be expressed as a single function:

// before Go 1.18
func SortInts(s []int) { /* ... */ }
func SortStrings(s []string) { /* ... */ }
// ...

// after Go 1.18
func Sort[E cmp.Ordered](s []E) { /* ... */ }

However, no such capability came to methods.

The generics proposal reasoned that because generic interface methods are difficult to implement efficiently (discussed later), it didn’t make sense to add type parameters to non-interface (or “concrete”) methods either. In that view, methods are primarily the means of implementing an interface.

Go 1.27 takes a different view and consequently adds generic methods to Go. In this post, we’ll explain this change of view and demonstrate some uses of this new feature.

Methods for organization

Methods enable organizing functionality around types. To illustrate, let’s reconsider the linked list from above (adding some conveniences):

type List[E any] struct {
    elem E
    next *List[E]
}
func NewList[E any](elems ...E) List[E] { /* ... */ }
func (List[E]) String() string { /* ... */ }

Suppose that one wanted to map this structure to hold a value of some other type, like a string. A method like ToString would do:

func (List[E]) ToString(f func(E) string) List[string] { /* ... */ }

By providing a “transform” function f, ToString can be customized with “off-the-shelf” routines.

For example, strconv.Itoa might work for a List[int]:

func main() {
    fmt.Println(NewList(1, 2, 3).ToString(strconv.Itoa)) // [1 2 3]
}

For a List[[]byte], more options come to mind (depending on the use case):

func main() {
    l := NewList([]byte("Hallo Welt"), []byte("Helló világ"))
    fmt.Println(l).ToString(hex.EncodeToString)                 // [48616c6c6f2057656c74 48656c6cc3b32076696cc3a167]
    fmt.Println(l).ToString(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString)  // [SGFsbG8gV2VsdA== SGVsbMOzIHZpbMOhZw==]
}

Note that parameterizing List allowed generalization of the source type, but not the destination type, since that depends on the transformation being applied. This might be reasonable with just a single destination type, but what if there were many?

In Go 1.18, a generic function could be used for this:

// after Go 1.18
func MapList[E, R any](l List[E], f func(E) R) List[R] { /* ... */ }

But using a function has the disadvantage of moving MapList into the package scope—if many data types support mapping operations, things could get crowded. Furthermore, chained calls must be written “inside out”:

func main() {
    fmt.Println(MapList(MapList(NewList(0, 2, 4), add(2)), divideBy(2))) // [1 2 3]
}

Because Go 1.18 didn’t support generic methods, we needed a generic function as a workaround. This is now remedied in Go 1.27:

// after Go 1.27
func (List[E]) Map[R any](f func(E) R) List[R] { /* ... */ }

This is compact, expressive, and locally scoped. Additionally, chained calls are more readable, as they can be written more naturally from left to right:

func main() {
    fmt.Println(NewList(0, 2, 4).Map(add(2)).Map(divideBy(2))) // [1 2 3]
}

Prefer the “inside out” form? A method expression can convert any method, including a generic one, into its function equivalent. Thus, a function call structure can be recovered if desired:

func main() {
    f := List[int].Map[int]
    fmt.Println(f(f(NewList(0, 2, 4), add(2)), divideBy(2))) // [1 2 3]
}

Generic methods, like other generics in Go, must be instantiated (either explicitly or implicitly) before they are used (called or converted to a function).

Decoupling things

If one views methods also as an organizational tool, then Go 1.18’s reasoning appears overly restrictive. While a generic concrete method can’t help implement an interface (without generic interface methods), it can still be useful for code organization. In other words, these concerns can be decoupled.

To elaborate, let’s consider a simple interface:

type I interface {
    M()
}
type T struct{}                   // a struct, not an interface
func (T) M[P any]() { /* ... */ } // a generic *concrete* method

Here, T.M is parameterized by P. Any instantiation of T.M would result in a method signature identical to that of I.M:

func main() {
    T{}.M[int]()
}

Both T.M[int] and I.M have the signature func M(). However, this doesn’t mean T implements I. Interface implementation is a property of a (possibly instantiated) type, not of any particular method. Importantly, T does not declare T.M[int], but rather its generic (and thus uninstantiated) counterpart T.M.

For T.M to participate in interface implementation, there would need to exist a suitable generic method on I.M:

type I interface {
    M[P any]() // a generic *interface* method
}
type T struct{}
func (T) M[P any]() { /* ... */ }

Since the Go 1.27 syntax doesn’t allow interface methods to declare type parameters, this code is impossible to write.

But why can’t Go have generic interface methods? To understand, a bit of a detour is needed.

The trouble with generic interface methods

An interface value is a box that can hold some other value—the boxed value can be of any type, as long as that type implements the interface. This means that the declared methods on the type are a superset of those declared on the interface.

To illustrate, T implements I below:

type I interface {
    M()
}
type T struct{}
func (T) M() { /* ... */ }

One can call methods on interface values:

func main() {
    F(T{})
}

func F(i I) {
    i.M() // "backed" by T.M
}

Above, it’s easy to observe that the call to i.M will be routed to T.M. But in more complex programs, the relation between an interface value method call and its possible targets is significantly less obvious. This relation typically spans across packages, making it difficult or impossible to deduce in the general case.

To illustrate, let’s introduce a package boundary:

// -- package main --
import "p"

func main() {
    p.F(T{})
}
type T struct{}
func (T) M() { /* ... */ }

// -- package p --
func F(i I) {
    i.M()
}
type I interface {
    M()
}

Because the two packages are compiled separately, the main package won’t know how p.F uses T{}. To ensure the existence of any method that p.F might call, the compiler generates code for all non-generic methods of a type at its declaration (or instantiation). That way, regardless of what p.F does with T{}, the necessary code will exist at runtime.

Now, suppose that I.M were generic:

// -- package main --
import "p"

func main() {
    p.F(T{})
}
type T struct{}
func (T) M[P any]() { /* ... */ }

// -- package p --
func F(i I) {
    i.M[int]()
}
type I interface {
    M[P any]()
}

Again, the main package won’t know how p.F uses T{}—including how it might instantiate T.M. To handle any usage of T{} inside p.F, the compiler would need to instantiate T.M with every possible type argument.

This is impractical with Go’s approach to instantiation, wherein the compiler generates specific code for each method based on the type arguments. If method arguments were “boxed” (i.e. passed as values of their constraint interfaces), each instantiation would share the same code. This would avoid having too many instantiations at the cost of indirect call overhead—even for direct calls to instantiated methods.

Conclusion

Go 1.27 introduces type parameters on concrete methods—this feature has been highly desired by the Go community, as it permits more ergonomic and readable code. Although we can’t support generic interface methods, we decided that allowing type parameters for concrete methods was still worthwhile.

We hope you enjoy using Go’s generic methods and find helpful ways to use them in your projects!

Previous article: Go 1.27 is released

content:
$5300 in $100s please. That's what we said at the bank this morning.

See, whenever you have a free IRL event, you tend to get a lot of no-shows. Plenty of people sign up and RSVP, but ultimately far fewer show up.

This isn't a big deal if you have unlimited space and anyone can just show, but if you want to have an event at a small venue, and you can only host, say, 80 people, you need to have a sense of how many are coming. That's why you require signup, that's why you require RSVPs.

But still, many don't show. We've run into this with our own free events over the years. You "sell out" of space, but you end up with 15 extra seats because people don't show. Those seats could have been filled with people who really wanted to be there. We could charge, which might help, but we really want this to be a free event.

So what to do? How can we find a way to bridge the gap between who says they'll show, and who will really show? How do we shrink the delta?

We're trying something tomorrow.

Tomorrow we have a Breakfast with Basecamp IRL event in Chicago. It's entirely free. As long as you show up.

When you register you're charged $100. And if you show up, you get a crisp $100 bill at the door. So you're made whole, it's entirely free. If you don't show, you forfeit your $100. It costs you money not to be there. A little incentive.

This isn't a new idea. Some restaurants have been charging for reservations, essentially asking you put down a deposit which can be applied to the meal if you show. If not, you lose the deposit.

So we're doing the same thing, except for a free event, and rather than apply the deposit to the meal or ticket price (which we don't have), we just literally hand you back the cost of admission, with a smile.

I'm really curious to see if it works. I'll comment back with the no-show rate and compare it to our last event where we didn't do this at all.

-Jason

content:
A lot of people have the wrong idea about fundraising.

They make fundraising a really complex thing, making it seem that you have to change your entire personality, or lie, or somehow try to fool people.

After Solo Founders and Y Combinator, I’ve realized that most of that is overcomplicating things.

There’s really only one thing you have to learn so you can fundraise successfully:

learn to think like a VC

When you have a good mental model of how a VC makes decisions will you be able to leverage that into a successful fundraise. Failing to create the right mental model is the number one problem most early-stage founders make.

Here are some VC-mentality principles, the implication of each, and how it should affect your mindset.

1. Giving money is the VC’s entire job, so never beg

This may sound surprising or obvious, but always remember:

VCs want to give startups money.

They don’t want to sit around and put their money in an index fund. They are just waiting for a founder to come in with incredible energy, a great product.

Because if they find the next Zuckerberg before anyone else, this means they get a share at the lowest valuation, and gain the most in subsequent rounds.

The practical implication is that you never should go into a VC call with a beggar mentality.

You instead want to become the person they believe in, feel inspired by, and want to see succeed (and thus give their money to.)

2. VCs work with incomplete information, so signal competency

Given the speed that VCs need to review and make decisions, they necessarily work based on incomplete information. After a point, every agentic AI startup starts sounding the same.

This means they’re using some common patterns or “signals” to evaluate startups. Here are some of them, in an approximate descending order of importance:

  • Accelerators – if you’re accepted into something like Solo Founders or Y Combinator, someone smart has made a bet on you already, and it’s easier to trust you.
  • Pedigree Alma Mater – same logic
  • Big Tech – their interviews are infamously hard, and if someone can crack that, you have higher chances of building a successful company than the average person
  • Warm Referrals – which means their friends like you or you are popular enough to be discussed
  • Social media / Github stars / other engagement signals – if a lot of people engage with your content, you have some idea how to distribute a product, and distribution is an important skill.

The implication here is that if your pitch is exclusively focusing on the technology without signalling in other ways, the VC might feel something missing.

3. VCs get 1000s of opportunities to invest, so stand out

Every VC has an inbox full of potential new companies to invest in.

This means that if you’re trying to raise funds by cold emailing VCs, you’re not going to have good chances.

The idea is to make the VC notice you and chase you, rather than the other way around, because chasing a VC will never work.

Now that’s not always simple – but one of the easiest ways is social media.

E.g. if you have all the VCs in your linkedin, it means that whenever you share progress updates, launch videos, or customer testimonials, the investor will notice you.

I have a first-hand experience of this: around demo day, my posts got liked by some VCs, which meant that other VCs in their network also saw my posts, and it became a self-fulfilling circle.

You can set something like that for yourself too. I created a completely free list of all the early stage investors in SF, preseed and seed, 500+ investors just waiting for you to come and wow them.

You can also use my tool to automate this connection to VCs. This is especially powerful for companies currently in an accelerator like YC – since you don’t have much time to do this manually, automating it can significantly increase your fundraise chances at demo day. Just visit gigacatalyst.com/multiplier/yc/investors and type in your company website.

4. VCs like to make you wait, so create urgency and close quick

Even though it seems tempting to go to that VC dinner or talk to that VC early, don’t take the bait.

They want an earlier conversation so they can extract information and make you an earlier deal on less competitive terms.

This actually happened when an investor came to my residence at 11pm in the night to make a shitty lowball offer. Fortunately I was able to call up one of the most legendary VCs in the city, @julianweisser, who helped me say no to that bad deal, otherwise I’d have given up a lot more of my company at a poorer valuation.

The solution is to compress all VC meetings to a span of 7 to 14 days and create a fast-moving competition where every VC feels FOMO to sign quickly or lose out.

Paul Graham famously regards Sam Altman to be one of the best at fundraising, and I had the pleasure of hearing this directly from him when he spoke at YC. Failing to create a competitive environment can truly be the #1 killer to your entire fundraise. He wrote an entire article on this topic, so go and read that one too.

Conclusion

When you start thinking like a VC, you’ll see that there’s genuinely no need for tricks.

Ultimately, it’s two humans making a business decision. VCs cannot exist without startups, but startups existed long before VCs.

So keep your head high and go get that bread.

What are your fundraising secrets (or mistakes) that you’ve made?

Keep shipping, Namanyay

content:
Modesty arguments often say that you should mostly or entirely bow to ‘expert consensus’ or the views of particular others, and who are you to disagree.

It has been a few years since I’ve properly addressed this so: My answer is that you are you. Other people are saying things for a wide variety of reasons, many of which are not about them paying attention and focusing on seeking this particular truth. Those people make mistakes all the time, and often have other motives and influences at work, especially social pressures and information cascades.

Them being as smart as you, or smarter than you, does not exempt them from this, and them being higher status or credentialed or cooler definitely does not exempt them.

A smart informed person sincerely thinking [X] can easily cease to be evidence for [X], once you have thought sufficiently about both [X] and why that person thinks [X].

Think for yourself, schmuck.

Or, as I once put it: You Have The Right To Think, also the moral duty to do so.

This post covers Eliezer Yudkowsky making a narrower claim than mine, about not conflating status with smarts and epistemic authority, and my documenting related discussion that happened on Twitter.

This concerns a particular historical interaction, but what matters is the general point.

I then briefly extend this to my broader claims.

Modesty’s Bailey

I think, in the exchange I will quote, Rob Bensinger is reaching but centrally correct.

Modesty arguments often are this, trying to conflate the motte and bailey as usual:

  1. Motte: You should treat the opinions and arguments of others as meaningful information, and take it into account as Bayesian evidence.
  2. Bailey: You cannot rationally weigh your inside view more than the views of others, or disagree much with expert consensus, or whoever is considered epistemically in charge around here, unless you can cite specific information you have that they don’t have access to. If you do, you are making a claim of high status, and that they are relatively stupid.

I affirm Modesty’s Motte.

I am heavily against Modesty’s Bailey.

Epistemic Peerage

Note the bolded passage (bold is mine) in the exchange below:

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Folks also don’t seem to realize that “epistemic peer” is a term of art in epistemology for people so impressive you’ll defer to them in your discipline without even needing to hear an argument. It doesn’t just mean “colleague you treat with respect”.​

It doesn’t mean you should mostly or fully defer to such a person. That would imply they are an ‘epistemic superior,’ someone whose opinion carries greater weight than your own, or even an ‘expert’ or ‘guru’ that you should defer to entirely except under special circumstances.

Epistemic peer means that, if you both have access to the same information, and they have not yet explained to you their reasoning, you should not presume one of you is better at this than the other, so you should probably take the two unadjusted opinions and split the difference.

Once they explain their reasoning, you should instead evaluate their reasoning. Sometimes they will have better reasoning than you, sometimes it will be worse. Remember the law of Conservation of Expected Evidence. If you could move towards their belief but not away from it, you should adjust your beliefs now.

The Exchange

I’m reproducing this discussion primarily because I think it has valuable things to say about how to do, and how not to do, epistemics, rather than because of the OP story being about Leopold in particular. Leopold, indeed, would later wisely recant the central conceptual point, in the form of creating the hedge fund Situational Awareness, whether or not he would agree that the two are the same principle.

Aashish Reddy: Eliezer on encountering Leopold, which some of you will enjoy:

Eliezer Yudkowsky (on LW): I remember the first time I met Leopold Aschenbrenner. He questioned me about why my timelines weren’t longer and finally said, “Why aren’t you updating at all in the direction of all the smart people saying longer timelines?” (aka: OpenPhil doctrine of 2050), “At this point you’re not even pretending to be rational.”

I hesitated briefly, because I knew it would not end well to answer honestly, but there wasn’t any good ending past there; and then I told him honestly that I did not consider those people to be my epistemic peers.

I don’t usually consider myself good at reading faces, but wow, the sheer LOOK of contempt and scorn that crossed his face; before he turned away and walked off without another word, dismissing me from further consideration. I will never forget that moment — because of it being such a LOUD face and my actually being able to read it, not because it had any influence on my estimates, of course.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: …and zero comments on the point that, in retrospect, Leopold appears to have been flat wrong that I ought to defer to his very respectable people about timelines, and my “Biological Anchoring: The Trick That Never Works” was ~100% correct? Cool. Y’all do you.

An obsession with vibes so grand that all grading of predictive outcomes is beneath it. How could you stand grandly above two people if you were also noticing that their predictions were not equally wrong? You cannot. So you are blind to the outcomes themselves.

Folks also don’t seem to realize that “epistemic peer” is a term of art in epistemology for people so impressive you’ll defer to them in your discipline without even needing to hear an argument. It doesn’t just mean “colleague you treat with respect”.

Oliver Habryka: I mean, I think the common-sense use of the term would have also been fine here? Like, it seems true and clear to me (from other things Eliezer has said) that he also does not consider them his epistemic peers in a more common-usage sense of the word.

Rob Bensinger: Seems vague, and dependent on interpretive details. And seems like an inference rather than an observation, and one that moves further away from the core of the disagreement with Leopold. (And if we readily read “epistemic peer” that way, we lose a very useful concept.)

Oliver Habryka: I mean, in as much as people’s reaction is to “broad disrespect for Leopold’s epistemics by Eliezers” then I think that reaction seems appropriate. I think it’s clear Eliezer does not have much respect for Leopold’s epistemics (and to be clear, neither do I).

Trying to invoke a misunderstanding about the term “epistemic peer”, feels like it’s a distraction in as much as that is the core disagreement.

Rob Bensinger: Leopold’s motte is “you should treat your colleagues with a modicum of respect and politeness”, and his bailey is “you should weight your own inside view no higher than Cotra’s, Carlsmith’s, etc.” Shrugging at the distinction lets him declare full victory.

Oliver Habryka: Is… it? I am confused. Is Leopold even participating in this conversation? Like, that was his motte with Eliezer? I don’t think so, or at least it doesn’t match my model of him, or the way he carries himself.

Rob Bensinger: This seems like a pretty general / common description of how modest epistemology works? You conflate the social hierarchy with the epistemic hierarchy; you conflate norms of collegiality with norms of deference, so that “arrogance” carries the moral valence of “being a dick”.

… And not just the valence of “being factually mistaken about some third party’s level of expertise”.

That’s where the outrage and force of Leopold’s action comes from, if Leopold’s mind is reasonably typical on this dimension. “How dare you BE SO RUDE”, not “… THINK 2+2=5”.

Oliver Habryka: Huh, I guess that doesn’t match my model of Leopold at all. Leopold dismisses almost everyone!

IMO the thing that Leopold was doing in that interaction (as I think I was there, or at least heard about it soon after) was demanding respect for the EA elders + the gods of the marketplace the way you demand respect for a king.

Rob Bensinger: I’m not sure I see how those things are incompatible with what I said? I think “show a modicum of professional courtesy to your colleagues” is often what “treat EA elders like they’re your kings” feels like from the inside.

Eliezer’s Explanation

Eliezer offers a fictionalized version that did not happen as written, but that to him illustrates the core thing that happened. He may or may not be right, I was not there.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: Let me translate [the OP Eliezer quote] out of Lesswrongese.

Leopold: Why do you think AGI could possibly happen as soon as 2030? The people *I* think are cool say 2050.

Eliezer: Blah blah actual reasons blah blah.

(History: Later shows my reasoning to be correct. You can read it in “Biology-Inspired AGI Timelines: The Trick That Never Works.”)

Leopold: But do you think you’re *smarter* than the people *I* think are cool and who put their median timelines at 2050? You should adjust your position toward their position, even if you disagree with their arguments, because you’re no smarter than them. That’s what *rational* people are supposed to do.

(History: Will later show all their arguments were wrong for exactly the reasons I said they would be wrong.)

Eliezer: If you are literally going to phrase it that way and try to put me in that kind of conversational corner, then fine, since I cannot win this conversation I will simply say what I believe to be true: Yes, I think I’m a sufficiently better forecaster that I’ve already taken their arguments into account, and that they haven’t understood my arguments, and so I trust my own decision not to treat them as authorities whose opinion I ought to weigh on par with my own.

(History: Good call.)

Leopold: CONTEMPT

Eliezer: (Says nothing for the next few years because at the time Leopold is just a punk kid; and even if I immediately suspect that he is EA-bait who will get promoted to a position of power and then do a lot of damage, he is right now just a punk kid, and if you are a senior guy with a little power, you don’t bring your own weight to bear against a kid.)

Leopold: (Gets promoted to a position of high power at eg FTX Philanthropy.) (Tries to torpedo my own suggestions and initiatives.) (After the ChatGPT moment makes it publicly acceptable and cool, switches to saying that AGI is coming in 2027 and we need to start an arms race with China about it.)

(Blows up a hedge fund.)

I should emphasize: This “translated” conversation DID NOT HAPPEN. Leopold did not say those things; I did not say those replies. The original on LessWrong is my best recollection of how the actual conversation went.

‘Blows up a hedge fund’ goes too far in describing what happened to Leopold’s hedge fund, Situational Awareness. It declined from $45 billion in assets to $10 billion, after it used too much leverage and got caught in margin calls, forcing a sale of its public book, but it did not per se blow up.

Leopold’s entire approach to his hedge fund did represent an extremely not-modest view of the world, to not only bet on his own ‘situational awareness’ and analysis of the market, but to do so at high leverage and for amounts where he was likely impacting prices, and thus vulnerable to additional pressures.

And you know what? He got too aggressive with leverage, but he was fundamentally right to be immodest, and to say he could better predict prices than the market, because he was looking closer, thinking better and more situationally aware. He made lots of great trades. The Efficient Market Hypothesis is False, and it is people like Leopold who make it do an imitation of true.

Man, Machine, Self: I think much of the heat came from them correctly correctly picking up, in non-lesswrong-ese, “saying someone is not your epistemic peer” sounds a lot like you’re insulting them and calling them stupid.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: There is a truth which destroys the minds of EAs; as hinted by Aumann and explicitly argued by Hanson, to not defer to someone’s authority, you must think you are smarter than them. This destroys people because their brain processes smartness as status.

Leopold tried to back me into a corner where to not defer to his friends, I had to speak the terrible, socially unutterable truth that I did not consider them just as smart as me. I bit the bullet and received his look of utter contempt in exchange — and was right, of course. But imagine how hard it is for most EA kids to decide that they are ready to do the same, when everyone around them is telling them to be humble and not to get above themselves. And that’s how and why OpenPhil was groupthink.

Zy (QTing the previous quote): Rationalist Hadith

QC: the most important thing i learned from rationalists is that smart people can be incredibly stupid. you have the god-given right to refuse to defer to anyone’s authority no matter how smart they seem if they’re talking nonsense, and intelligence is no substitute for wisdom.

Eliezer Yudkowsky: …And now people who have no word for what I mean by “smart” are naturally reading it as the status thing. But of course they have no word for it, so I was foolish to call it “smart” instead of “shmeerp”, a sum of knowledge and accurate self-assessment of relative validity by which you’d correctly decide that it was fine for *you* to decide the AGI-2050 arguments were trash even though *other people* thought those arguments were *not* trash.

The truth that destroys EAs is that you’ve got to believe you’ve got higher shmeerp than the AGI-2050 crowd to shrug off their arguments; and obviously whatever the heck shmeerp is, it would be very high-status to have it; so they think it’s terribly rude to say outright that you think you have higher shmeerp than high-status other people — and *they* often do actually usually just say “smart”, there.

And then they are lost, because shmeerp does not track their sense of what status MUST be in order for the universe to MAKE SENSE, and so they have to redistribute shmeerp and reinterpret the whole universe of arguments accordingly, following by unseeing the universe.

And that’s how OpenPhil ended up believing in AGI 2050 while simultaneously and to this very day earnestly congratulating themselves on how they were great at avoiding groupthink.

A Demonstration That Eliezer’s Translation Accurately Describes Many People Whether Or Not It Describes Leopold

As in, here is someone else’s pejorative translation of events, which confirms it.

Will Rinehart:

>be Eliezer “I invented Bayesian rationality” Yudkowsky
>meet young Leopold who actually works on the frontier
>kid asks “why aren’t you updating at all in the direction of all the smart people?”
>you hesitate for dramatic effect, then drop the ultimate high-IQ line:
>”I do not consider those people to be my epistemic peers”
>Leopold’s face contorts into pure, unfiltered contempt
>he turns and walks away without another word
>you stand there alone, triumphant
>”wow, I actually managed to read a facial expression for once. historic day”
>this of course has zero impact on your probability estimates because peers are for midwits

This is exactly the attitude Eliezer is describing:

  1. If you do take your opinion into account more than someone else, you are calling them stupid. More than that, you are claiming ‘ultimate high-IQ.’
  2. Status in context should largely equate to smartness.
  3. Learning that [X] is high status should update you towards [X]’s opinion, even if you had already considered [X]’s arguments.

Pay attention to both the literal contents, and also to the vibe of utter contempt, not only from Leopold but also from Will Rinehart.

As in, contempt for the idea that anyone might think for themselves, or consider arguments rather than who else believes what.

Will’s contempt persists, despite Eliezer being vindicated on the substance.

Later, of course, Leopold wisely got over it, and indeed took it too far.

Wrong, Stupid and Low Status Are Three Distinct Things

Most people only partially make the relevant mistake.

Each correlates with the others, but mostly people know they are distinct.

It is most common to equate calling someone wrong and calling someone stupid.

  1. Only a stupid person would be so wrong.
  2. You would only dare think they were wrong if you thought they were stupid.
  3. You would only dare call them wrong if you thought they were stupid.
  4. You know that calling them wrong will be heard as calling them stupid.

Whereas, of course, smart people are wrong about things all the time, and stupid people are right about things all the time. Sometimes the smart person is wrong, and the stupid person is right, or the smart group is wrong and the stupid group is right, either because or in spite of superior information.

The other links are usually seen as more tenuous.

Of course people constantly use accusations of stupidity or wrongness to try and lower someone’s status, or smartness and rightness to raise it. Most people in most places still push back hard against attempts to too systematically equate smart or right with high status, or especially stupid and wrong with low status. We realize they are not the same, and also the monkey brain knows that there be dragons.

The danger comes in places that do systematically equate intelligence and rightness with status. Academia is the most famous version of this.

LessWrong-Yudkowsky style rationality has this as an obvious failure mode. You have to constantly push back against where the high status person says ‘think for yourself’ and everyone says ‘yes, as the guru says we will think for ourselves exactly as he told us to.’ There is no amount of hammering ‘no I am not a guru, at most I am an epistemic superior, I really am saying to think for yourselves’ or ‘we are not a cult’ that will consistently fully stick. In my experience rationalist circles manage, after much effort, to do a good overall job at this, but not a great one.

Effective Altruism is set up to have a maximally bad version of this mistake. There is tons of pressure to quantify all the things, and to maximize quantified results, and to bow to the legible, and a lot of demand to be told how to figure out how to think and do in order to do the most good, and thus be good, and so on. Results are often prioritized over epistemics. This all puts extra value on consensus, and various forms of high status often end up equated with correctness or intelligence or both.

(As usual, to avoid related implications, my caveat that while EA has lots of issues, we criticize them so much exactly because they are worth taking the effort to criticize, and if you don’t believe that you should see the other guy.)

A Quick Survey Of Some Reasons To Not Be Epistemically Modest

The essence of my broader claim is that, in practice, modesty arguments get screened off by sufficient attention and understanding. Modesty is a method for when you cannot budget sufficient attention and understanding, which is most of the time.

You Have The Right To Think. See that post, and also the extended discussions in the comments between me and, among others, Eliezer Yudkowsky and Robin Hanson.

The post was initially motivated as a response to Robin Hanson’s review of Eliezer’s highly related book Inadequate Equilibria, which discusses when you might be able to do something unusually well.

Actual modesty, in practice, happens for a mix of complicated reasons, as I broke down in On Robin Hanson’s ‘Social Proof, But Of What?’.

Once you have invested enough to understand the relevant questions and form an opinion, and have considered the arguments and other causes behind people’s opinions, you can and should substitute your judgment for theirs.

Often you should do this despite the ‘experts’ or other epistemic would-be authorities having more relevant knowledge than you, and having devoted more time to related questions than you, outnumbering you, being higher status and more respected and credentialed than you, and perhaps being smarter than you.

Your investment of sufficient attention and understanding can be and often is fractal. As illustrated in Leaders of Men, you can confidently point out where an expert, who knows ball far better than you, is failing to properly understand an aspect of ball. In Zeroing Out, I explain how you can know a consensus estimate is wrong in a particular direction, even if you could not hope to create, on your own, an estimate as accurate as the consensus.

This, ideally along with a track record of testable predictions and the logic behind them, gives you many tools by which to evaluate whether someone, or some group, is functionally an epistemic peer or superior in a given context.

The obvious mistake is ‘I disagree with them, therefore they are not an epistemic peer,’ which would defeat the whole purpose. What you can and should do is adjust your evaluation of sources based on the quality of their arguments.

This blog has always been about not being epistemically modest, most famously:

Zvi Mowshowitz (February 9, 2021): I fully reject the idea that smart people can’t improve on the margin on ‘expert’ opinion, period. Welcome to 2021. Modesty shmodesty.

Covid-19 and our response to it demonstrated, basically, ‘modesty shmodesty.’ AI only pushed me further in that direction. I now have an extensive track record to look through, and see how things are going.

There is also an extensive track record regarding claims around AI timelines, the topic of the original exchange between Eliezer and Leopold. We have seen many, including Leopold, radically shorten their timelines (Leopold as late as August 2021 was only estimating 25% chance of AGI-level systems by 2070), based on evidence that was mostly foreseeable in advance, combined with shifting social context.

Against Modesty’s Bailey

To close, here is a quick list of the top 10 reasons to decide to disagree with an expert or general consensus, either locally or globally, including a market price, or with others who might otherwise be presumed to know better.

  1. You know something they don’t, or know unique reasons you can trust key info.
  2. You have devoted more attention to something relevant than they have.
  3. They have not priced in or understood your reasons or reasoning.
  4. You checked, and their reasoning is bad and they should feel bad.
  5. No, seriously, often the reasoning is really dumb, or obviously motivated.
  6. Social desirability and other biases impacting the consensus.
  7. Information cascades and games of telephone distorting consensus.
  8. You can explain their statements in other ways that do not track truth, and your model predicts they would say that even if it was false.
  9. They seem to be lying to you, including ‘for your own good’ or the ‘common good.’
  10. The demands for modesty and adherence to a particular epistemic authority are selective and asymmetrical. Why are you supposed to adhere to this particular person or group, rather than others?

On top of the reasons to not be epistemically modest, there are strong reasons to state your immodest beliefs: It is often more helpful to present your own views and your own reasons, rather than to mirror everyone else, to combat the reasons above.

Thus, I reaffirm Modesty’s Motte and re-reject Modesty’s Bailey.

Trying to update my extensions didn't work. I still got that error. The only thing that worked was to downgrade to VS Code v1.124.2. This also undid the redesign that I kinda hate.

Obviously keeping things at this older version of VS Code is not a viable strategy, so maybe this issue will actually be fixed instead of just being closed for no reason.

content:
Someone on the VS Code team decided to do a redesign of the product. This makes VS Code look like this:

This design is fine, I guess? It's got some rounded corners that look nice, I guess, but I really just want it to look like what I'm used to. I can tolerate this kind of redesign in my chat app, but I use VS Code professionally and kinda want things to look the same so I don't have to think as much.

You can revert the design change by setting "workbench.experimental.modernUI": false in your settings.json. Then it looks like this:

Who knows how long this is going to last, but at the very least it should work for now.

Thanks to jtagcat and Hugo ARNAL for letting me know about this setting.
